item.title: In focus on protein intake, don’t forget about dietary fibre
item.description: Dietary fibre has health benefits and can also help to keep you feeling fuller for longer after a meal.
item.content:encoded:
Protein has been everywhere lately. You may have seen food products promoting high protein content, or reels online telling you how to boost your intake.

One of the ways protein supports our health is by helping a meal fill us up (satiation) and keeping us feeling fuller for longer between meals (satiety). It does this by influencing our appetite hormones and other metabolic processes.

But protein is not the only nutrient that helps with satiation and satiety. And if we focus too much on protein, we may miss the big picture and forget about other important nutrients.

It’s time to put the spotlight on dietary fibre and where to get it – especially as most of us aren’t eating enough.

Let’s take a look at how much protein you need, how much fibre, and how they compare in keeping you feeling full.

First, do we really need more protein?

The recommended dietary intake of protein for Australian adults aged 19–70 years is 46 grams a day for women and 64g a day for men.

Across your day, this could look like eating:

  • 200 millilitres of natural yoghurt (10.6g protein)

  • a beef burger (31.5g protein)

  • 20g almonds (3.9g protein)

  • and for men – an extra 75g of cooked chicken thigh (18.2g protein).

item.title: ‘The Catcher in the Rye’ is 75, and every time I meet Holden Caulfield, I see him anew
item.description: One of the most convincing things about Salinger’s novel is its rendition of the idiom of a teenager who is perhaps not quite as jaded as he thinks he is.
item.content:encoded:
Reading The Catcher in the Rye in high school once carried a certain edgy credibility. Holden Caulfield was the embodiment of youthful alienation for generations of readers and critics. Novelist Joseph O’Connor recalls how, “like many teenaged readers”, he “felt like Holden was talking to me – perhaps to me alone” on first reading the novel in 1981.

This was the obvious irony of readers’ identification with JD Salinger’s teenage loner: if everyone identifies with him, how unique is he really? Perhaps every teenager has at least a few hours where they think of themselves as singular, authentic, misunderstood.

But The Catcher in the Rye turned 75 this year. Holden would now be in his 90s, and identifying with him has become less fashionable. Readers in the 21st century are more likely to skewer him for unchecked privilege, viewing his disaffection as a form of affluenza tied to wealth and whiteness. Even those whose backgrounds and circumstances resemble Holden’s may struggle to sympathise with a character so oblivious to his advantages.

Surely, Holden has it all: high-end luggage, brand-new ice skates, wads of spending money, a series of fresh starts at different private schools. His father “haul[s] it in” as a corporate lawyer. A rich boy enjoying the luxury of self-sabotage in the name...

item.title: Extreme poverty in India falls to 2.6%, but top 10% earn 13 times more than bottom 10%: World Bank
item.description: The international financial institution sets the international extreme poverty line at $3 a day.
item.content:encoded:
India’s extreme poverty rate fell from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023, the World Bank has said in its October Poverty and Equity Brief. However, it added that income disparities remain wide, with the top 10% of the population earning a median income about 13 times more than the bottom 10%.

The World Bank sets the international extreme poverty line at $3 a day, or roughly Rs 284.9 per day.

“As poverty declined, it became increasingly concentrated among households with lower education, fewer assets, limited access to stable employment, and higher dependency ratios,” said the World Bank.

It added that the share of India’s population living below the lower-middle-income poverty line of $4.2, or Rs 398.8 a day, fell from 57.7% in 2011 to 16.1% in 2023, with an estimated 49.6 crore people moving out of poverty.

The World Bank attributed the decline mainly to “strong consumption growth, rising employment, especially among women and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies”.

Poverty also declined on non-monetary measures. The Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative’s Multidimensional Poverty Index fell to 16.4% in 2019-’21 from 53.8% in 2005-’06. The World Bank’s own measure put multidimensional poverty at 15.5% in 2022-’23.

item.title: Sri Lanka mourns beloved gentle giant amid calls for better elephant conservation
item.description: The death of Kavantissa triggered an extraordinary wave of public grief, political attention and criticism of wildlife authorities.
item.content:encoded:
The death of Kavantissa, one of Sri Lanka’s most iconic wild tuskers (Elephas maximus maximus), following a gunshot injury triggered an extraordinary wave of public grief, political attention and criticism of wildlife authorities. The elephant’s final days brought together politicians, Buddhist monks, wildlife enthusiasts and veterinarians in a collective effort to save a giant that had captured the hearts of many Sri Lankans.

A photograph of Sri Lanka’s opposition leader Sajith Premadasa, an ardent elephant enthusiast kissing the elephant’s head went viral on social media as did the environment minister Dhammika Patabendi visiting the elephant amidst heavy rain.

Buddhist monks chanted Pirith (traditional Buddhist verses to invoke blessings), while a prominent businessman Dudley Sirisena offered to fund treatment, including a foreign veterinary team being flown in. Former president Mahinda Rajapaksa was among those who paid tribute to the magnificent tusker as well.

Despite the intensive efforts of wildlife veterinarians, Kavantissa suffered cardiac arrest on the evening of October 16.

Senior wildlife veterinary surgeons were present, and one reportedly climbed onto his chest in an attempt to administer cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). Their efforts failed, and the tusker died at around 6.18 pm.

item.title: ‘Wicker’ review: An exquisitely crafted fairy tale romance
item.description: Directed and written by Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson, the film stars Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgard.
item.content:encoded:
In a village sometime in the past somewhere in England, people are known by their professions – the Butcher, the Bottlewasher. Married women are simply known as the wives of so and so. At weddings, a metal collar replaces the bridal bouquet.

The Fisherwoman who lives in a hut on the edge of the village isn’t anybody’s wife. She is just Fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) – orphaned, single and mocked for her slovenly appearance and body odour.

Fisherwoman is getting on in age too. After a particularly nasty episode, she marches to the Basket Weaver (Peter Dinklage) and demands that he make her a spouse. The result is the Wicker Husband (Alexander Skarsgard). This striking creation, built out of the wood of the willow, has the leonine face of the Beast from Jean Cocteau’s Beauty and the Beast, the manner of a Victorian gentleman and a body that creaks when it moves but is perfect in every other way.

Wicker Husband inspires shock and then envy, especially among the various wives who are stuck with boring, underperforming husbands. Tailor’s Wife (Elizabeth Debicki) is especially upset about Fisherwoman’s turn of fortune, and the effect that Wicker Husband is having on the women and the men of the village.

item.title: UP SIR: Supreme Court asks EC to take steps against bulk filing of Form 7s to delete voters
item.description: The poll panel acknowledged that such applications had been submitted in bulk but claimed that no action had been taken on them.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Friday asked the Election Commission to take “corrective steps” against Form 7 applications filed in bulk to delete voters’ names during the special intensive revision in Uttar Pradesh, reported Bar and Bench.

Form 7 is used to object to the inclusion of a name or seek the deletion of an existing name from the electoral roll.

During the hearing, a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked the petitioners to submit a note detailing the alleged irregularities in the voter roll revision process in Uttar Pradesh to the poll panel.

It directed the Election Commission to examine “the factual aspects” of the allegations and file a compliance report before the court.

This came after the advocate appearing for the poll panel acknowledged that Form 7 applications had been submitted in bulk during the special intensive revision, Live Law reported.

However, he said no action had been taken on the applications, as they were found to be false.

The petitioners disputed the poll panel’s claim, saying that 32 voter deletion applications had been filed against members of a “particular community” in one constituency. They added that two of these forms were signed by booth-level officers.

item.title: Fiction: The death of her father brings an estranged Meher back to her family manor in the hills
item.description: An excerpt from ‘In the Moonlit Kingdom’, by Aishwarya Jha.
item.content:encoded:
Old houses were the best keepers of secrets. Their realtor, Arta, stated it like a personal triumph, pulling back the trellised grate of the elevator. Adrien smiled appreciatively, but she was disconcerted. The sensation followed her to the ninth-floor apartment, the points of the parquet flooring drilling into her feet, the palm motifs on the glass doors growing dangerously engorged.

“You can see right to the Hofburg from here,” exulted Adrien, his long strides spanning all the rooms at once. “Did you notice the induction stove?”

The commute was short. The oversized vintage Chesterfield they had bought on a whim would fit just right in the living room. She stood at the bay window, the activities of a Lilliputian fairyland unfolding below. The light was perfect, scooping out the walls in elegant cascades. Illuminating but not overpowering. An artist’s dream. But dreams came in pairs, the nightmare never far behind. He didn’t know. No one knew what lurked under the eaves, in unseen corners, hovering beneath the decades…

Singh had been arrested in the case on November 1 and was granted bail by the Patna High Court in March, reported PTI.

The bail had been challenged by JD(U) MLC Neeraj Kumar, who is the grandson of Yadav.

On Friday, a bench of Justices MM Sundresh and Prasanna B Varale cancelled the bail granted to Singh and directed the Bihar Police to complete the investigation within four months, reported The Indian Express.

Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Friday said that a Uniform Civil Code would be implemented in Uttar Pradesh if the Bharatiya Janata Party retains power in the 2027 Assembly elections, The Indian Express reported.

“UCC has already been implemented in many states,” the newspaper quoted the BJP leader as saying. “If you form the BJP government in Uttar Pradesh, we will implement UCC in Uttar Pradesh.”

Shah made the remarks while addressing party colleagues at the BJP’s working committee meeting in Lucknow, PTI reported.

The Uniform Civil Code proposed by the BJP aims to introduce a common set of laws governing marriage, divorce, succession and adoption for all citizens. Currently, such personal affairs of different religions are based on community-specific laws, largely derived from their religious scriptures.

Introducing a common personal law has for long been on the BJP’s agenda and several states ruled by the party have been making advances towards implementing it.

The announcement on Friday follows Shah’s September statement that governments led by the BJP and its National Democratic Alliance partners in 21 states would introduce the Uniform Civil Code before 2029, when the next Lok Sabha elections are scheduled.

item.title: Flood alerts, evacuations in Bengal, Assam after Bhutan glacial lake outburst
item.description: The flood water from the Sintaphu lake in Bhutan was predicted to flow downstream into India.
item.content:encoded:
A flood caused by a glacial lake outburst in Bhutan on Thursday prompted the authorities in West Bengal and Assam to issue flash flood alerts for districts along major rivers and evacuate persons in vulnerable areas downstream.

In West Bengal, Cooch Behar, Tufanganj and Busirhat districts along the Sankosh river and its tributaries were on high alert, Reuters reported.

In Assam, settlements along the Brahmaputra river were also asked to remain alert, The Indian Express reported.

Glacial lake outburst floods occur when a lake fed by glacial melt breaches suddenly.

Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said the state was monitoring the impact of the glacial lake outburst in vulnerable areas of Dhubri and Kokrajhar districts.

The state’s teams were coordinating with the National Disaster Response Force and other agencies, Sarma said on social media. “Residents are requested to stay alert, follow official updates and cooperate with local officials,” he added.

West Bengal Water Resources Minister Nisith Pramanik said that persons living near tea gardens in the northern part of the state and riverbeds “must evacuate immediately”, reported The Indian Express.

The glacial lake outburst occurred in the Sintaphu lake near Wakila mountain in Bhutan.

item.title: A new book of investigative reporting finds out how Jamtara became India’s ‘phishing capital’
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Jamtara Calling: The Underbelly of Cybercrime’, by Chitradeep Chakraborty.
item.content:encoded:
Some years ago, cyber fraudsters drained Rs 23 lakh from the account of Preneet Kaur, former member of Parliament and wife of the former chief minister of Punjab, Amarinder Singh.

The callers from Jamtara hit upon her number by chance. Kaur, then an MP from Patiala, was in Delhi and had just left her residence to attend the day’s session in Parliament. The caller introduced himself as the manager of the bank branch where her salary was credited. On the pretext that her account had been marked as dormant because she had not withdrawn money for some time, he said her KYC needed an urgent update and asked for her ATM card details. In a rush, the MP shared all her details with the caller. As soon as they got hold of her banking information and the OTP, Rs 23 lakh disappeared within minutes. A complaint was lodged at the Parliament Street Police Station, and both Delhi and Punjab Police started an investigation.

item.title: ‘Meethe Mein Kya Hai’ review: A pleasant and safe Diwali offering
item.description: Radhika Bansal’s debut feature is out on Netflix.
item.content:encoded:
In a mansion in Lucknow, the matriarch known only as Nani (Rohini Hattangadi) is getting ready to welcome her brood for Diwali. Everybody turns up with emotional baggage in tow.

Nani’s grandson Jai (Ritwik Bhowmik) hasn’t fully recovered from the recent death of his wife. Jai’s mother Amrita (Ayesha Raza), her husband Ajay (Gaurav Sharma), Amrita’s brother Rishab (Abhay Kaul) and his wife Preeti (Tarana Raja) worry about how Nani is managing all by herself.

Amrita and Ajay also have their daughter Sana (Dalai) to be concerned about. Sana has confirmed her flitty reputation by getting married to Karam (Vikram Bakshi) without bothering to inform her family.

Sana’s staggering, and implausible, thoughtlessness serves as the spark that ignites mild fires in Meethe Mein Kya Hai. Writer-director Radhika Bansal’s pleasant and safe feature debut, which is out on Netflix, is keen on moving on from inexplicable behaviour and the past.

The Hindi film is a mesh of deftly handled observational humour and pretend drama. A neighbour’s 13-year-old daughter Meera (Shivika Rishi), who randomly happens to be crashing at Nani’s – there is really no shortage of space here – develops a bond with Jai that sets off alarm bells that nobody in the film hears.

item.title: ‘Akka’ review: An engrossing bejewelled catfight
item.description: Keerthy Suresh and Radhika Apte lead Dharmaraj Shetty’s Netflix series.
item.content:encoded:
The Netflix series Akka is set in the fictitious kingdom Pernuru somewhere in the Deccan swathe. Women have ruled Pernuru for generations. A matriarchy has dealt patriarchy a body blow by dispensing with marriage altogether.

The very notion of family is fluid here. The warrior queens take partners and casual lovers without bothering to add mangalsutras to their sizeable jewellery collections. The line of succession is female. Women hold the purse strings and wield the guns. If the men feel like pieces of furniture and therefore emasculated, that is too bad.

Even after Independence in 1947, Pernuru has held on to its privileges. The word of Muthakka (Monika Panwar and later Tanvi Azmi), one of the three rulers of Pernuru, controls the main industry, liquor brewing. By 1985, Bhavani (Keerthy Suresh) is in charge.

The party-pooper is another woman. Rudra (Radhika Apte) is dispatched to Pernuru by the Mumbai gangster Shankar (Mahesh Manjrekar) to wrest control of the liquor trade from the fearsome Bhavani. A fierce contest breaks out between the ruthless outsider and the duty-bound legatee.

item.title: In her art, Jayasri Burman shows how India’s old stories still speak to the present
item.description: Women occupy the centre as bearers of memory, tenderness and transformation.
item.content:encoded:
In the studio where Jayasri Burman works, the women enter already carrying what the stories have asked of them. They move forward with long dark hair that frames each face differently yet remains recognisable, and with a gaze that looks past the viewer into a time that has not finished speaking. For decades Burman has painted them not as illustrations of finished tales but as agents that still answer the present.

Born in Kolkata in 1960, the second daughter of the founder of the footwear giant Khadim, Burman grew up in a prosperity that never accounted for the pull of the epics her mother and aunts recited while the city prepared for Durga.

Her uncle Sakti Burman lived between India and France. Viewers still look for his hand in hers. She has never denied the kinship, yet nothing was simply inherited. Her first marriage, which had been arranged, lasted 17 years. Leaving it, she has said, felt like a bird released from a cage. Paresh Maity became her companion. In a household of painters, they complete what the other leaves open.

item.title: Israel elections: Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc finishes ahead, but short of majority
item.description: The prime minister’s alliance alleged that Arab-Israeli groups received foreign funding to influence the vote, which the poll panel described as ‘groundless’.
item.content:encoded:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s alliance finished ahead in the country’s general election, but was short of forming a majority.

Netanyahu’s coalition of right-wing and far-right parties won 53 of the 120 seats in Parliament.

The Opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, secured 48 seats. The Arab parties, which are supported largely by Israel’s Palestinian minority, won 19 seats.

A party or an alliance needs 61 seats to form the government.

As neither alliance secured a majority, the Arab parties were being viewed as kingmakers. The coalition talks were beginning and could last weeks.

Another election would be held if coalition talks fail and no government can be formed.

Before the polls, both alliances had said they would not form coalitions with two Arab parties, Raam and the Joint List.

On Thursday, Netanyahu’s bloc alleged that Arab-Israeli groups received foreign funding to influence the vote. The controversy centred on allegations that Raam received money from Qatar for the purpose. The accusations were rejected by both Arab parties and Qatar, AFP reported.

Dean Livne, the acting director general for the Electoral Commission, was quoted as having said that allegations of widespread irregularities in the conduct of the polls was “entirely groundless”.

item.title: What kind of cities is India’s infrastructure rush building?
item.description: Between all the metros, highways and riverfronts, India is building the pieces of cities faster than designing the relationships between them.
item.content:encoded:
I have spent much of my professional life looking at cities from two directions: India, where I grew up, and New York, where I now practice architecture and urban design.

This has made one thing clear: cities do not become successful because they possess the right collection of infrastructure. They become successful because their infrastructure, land, housing, economy, public spaces and institutions work in relationship with one another.

This distinction matters enormously for India today. The country is entering one of the largest episodes of urbanisation in its history. The World Bank estimates that India’s urban population could rise from roughly 480 million in 2020 to 951 million by 2050.

India is building metros, expressways, airports, industrial corridors, housing, logistics infrastructure and digital systems at a pace that would have been difficult to imagine a generation ago.

But what kind of city are we building through all this infrastructure?

Infrastructure is not the same thing as urbanism – the unique social and cultural patterns that emerge when residents of a city interact with their built and natural environments.

India’s problem may not be that it is building too little. It may be that we are building the pieces of the city faster than we are designing the relationships between them.

item.title: ‘Pyre’ review: A moving tale of loneliness and endurance
item.description: Vinod Kapri’s film, starring first-time actors Heera Devi and Padam Singh, is out in cinemas.

In a hilltop village in the Kumaon region, an elderly couple contemplate death by suicide. The landscape that provides gorgeous backdrops and towering trees has failed to shelter Tulsi (Heera Devi) and Padam (Padam Singh) from gnawing loneliness.

Tulsi and Padam have been married for over 60 years. Their only son Harish left the village years ago, never to return. There is little to look forward to for the goat herders except an unchanging routine and deteriorating health. The village has all but emptied out, with only a few neighbours left, who have to be summoned by blowing on a trumpet.

A bout of illness means an arduous trek to a health centre that is miles away. The couple bicker in an endearing way, and their love for each other is undiminished by age, but the remoteness of their dwellings is wearing them down.

item.title: Ireland mulls language test for citizenship. It will increase pressure on teaching resources
item.description: Any new requirement would need investment, enough teachers and better coordination to ensure people can access the language support they need.
item.content:encoded:
Anti-immigrant sentiment in Ireland has increased alongside concerns about the cost of living, public services and migrant integration. Against this backdrop, the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration is considering changes to the requirements for naturalisation. People applying for citizenship may be required to demonstrate language proficiency as part of the naturalisation process.

Under the proposed reforms, applicants will be required to demonstrate proficiency in English, Irish or Irish Sign Language. This could have consequences for the provision of classes teaching English for speakers of other languages (known as ESOL) in Ireland.

ESOL classes in Ireland have primarily supported integration, participation and access to employment. There were more than 36,900 non-national learners enrolled in 2024, and 4,572 ESOL courses delivered in the first 11 months of 2025.

If language skills become a condition of citizenship, the level of English required will need to be determined. There are also questions about who will provide the education and support needed to meet this requirement. This change has the potential to reshape the role and purpose of ESOL significantly. Any new requirement would need investment, enough teachers and better coordination to ensure people can access the language support they need.

item.title: Samuel Beckett’s ‘Happy Days’ has new meaning in the age of climate change
item.description: ‘Happy Days’ serves as a necessary reminder to look after our planet while we still can – if we are to avoid our bodies becoming engulfed by disaster.
item.content:encoded:
In Happy Days, one of Irish playwright Samuel Beckett’s best-known plays, the body of the protagonist Winnie is embedded in a mound of sand or dirt. During the first act, she is buried to her waist and in the second, she is buried up to her neck.

In the stage directions, Beckett specifies the staging should feature an “expanse of scorched grass rising centre to low mound”, as well as “blazing light”. This is suggestive of a post-human landscape which has been affected by ecological disaster.

Beckett’s works have been labelled absurd, existentialist, modern and postmodern by critics. Yet the setting presented in Happy Days (first performed in 1961) feels uniquely contemporary in our age of ongoing climate crisis.

Born in Dublin in 1906, some of Beckett’s earliest interactions with nature took place on local walks. Often joining his father William on lengthy excursions around the Dublin hills to avoid the religious obligation of Sunday church, these early ambles helped to imprint the landscape on his artistic consciousness. Images from these walks subsequently found their way into a number of his literary works.

item.title: Podcast: From race to caste and gender, Ramachandra Guha on arguments with Gandhi
item.description: The historian tells host Dinyar Patel why it is impossible to assign neat black-and-white binaries to the Mahatma and his ideas
item.content:encoded:
Was Mahatma Gandhi a racist? Did he support the caste system? Do his various arch-critics over the years – Dalit activists, Hindutva supporters, Marxists, and intellectuals ensconced in their ivory towers – have valid points?

Perhaps. With Gandhi, however, there are never easy answers. During his lifetime, Gandhi warmly encouraged criticism and debate. After his death, and despite all of the posthumous veneration and encomiums, the Mahatma has remained a lightning rod for controversy. In this episode of Past Imperfect, Ramachandra Guha takes us through these controversies to help us separate fact from fiction.

In Arguments with Gandhi, his latest book, Guha states that it is impossible to assign neat black-and-white binaries to the Mahatma and his ideas. “The geographical range of Gandhi’s life, the thematic range of his activities and the furious arguments his work evoked (and continues to evoke) make him a figure without parallel in the modern world,” he writes.

item.title: SIR: Around 1,600 foreigners identified on voter rolls in six states, reports ‘Hindustan Times’
item.description: While launching the the exercise in 2025, the poll panel said that ‘inclusion of names of foreign illegal immigrants’ was one of the reasons for conducting SIR.
item.content:encoded:
About 1,600 persons identified as foreign citizens were found on electoral rolls in six states during the special intensive revision, the Hindustan Times reported on Thursday.

After the voter roll revision, the six states have about 9.86 crore electors.

While launching the first phase of the exercise in June 2025, the Election Commission said that the “inclusion of the names of foreign illegal immigrants” was one of the reasons for conducting the revision.

The Hindustan Times sent queries to the chief electoral officers of 26 states and Union territories where the special intensive revision had been completed or draft rolls had been published. The officials from 11 states responded.

item.title: A new book revisits the years when Bombay’s working-class libraries were flourishing

As Bombay expanded in the late 19th century and early 20th century, it developed a strong library culture, which came to be organised along various lines – religious communities, neighbourhoods, and secular educational institutions.

On the one hand, there were community-led libraries, such as the Mulla Firoz Library (established in 1830), containing books relating to Zoroastrian religion, the Jain Reading Room and Library, the Jamestji Nasarwanji Petit Fore Reading Room and Library by Parsis, the MJ Khoja Library and the Anjuman-i-Islam by Muslims. On the other hand, there were strong neighbourhood libraries, such as the Native General Library (established in 1845) in Dhobi Talao and Sr D Petit Khanda Mohalla Library in Nizampura.

Some of these libraries were free and open to all; others charged a fee. The Special Intensive Revision of India’s voter rolls has sparked concerns about the widespread disenfranchisement of eligible voters and that it is becoming a citizenship test. Its method is not new, but what is different this time is that it threatens the right to vote.

Digital tools have served the rolls since the 1990s: voter identity cards from 1993, computerised rolls, voting machines in every constituency by the 2004 general election and photo rolls nationwide by 2009. Through those years, rolls were corrected one application at a time, with officers deciding each case – former Chief Election Commissioner SY Quraishi says they were already about 99% accurate. From 2015 the Commission set out to “purify” the rolls by matching them against Aadhaar records.

The SIR, which began in Bihar in June 2025, completes the turn. It denies the roll on which the 2024 general election was held any presumption of eligibility, and presumes eligible only those found on a roll two decades old, so that everyone under about 40 can be linked only through a parent or grandparent or by producing supporting documents.

item.content:encoded:
As the Ganga water-sharing treaty between India and Bangladesh ends this year, Bihar seeks to resolve its long-standing demands before the treaty is renewed.

The treaty, signed in December 1996, governs the sharing of the Ganga river’s water between upstream India and downstream Bangladesh, particularly during the lean season when river flows are low.

Under the treaty, during the lean period from January to June, if water at the Farakka barrage is less than 70,000 cubic feet per second (cusecs), India and Bangladesh each get half. If the water at the barrage is between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, Bangladesh will be assured 35,000 cusecs, and the rest will go to India. If the water is 75,000 cusecs or more, India will get an assured 40,000 cusecs, and Bangladesh will get the rest.

The agreement further says Bangladesh will get a guaranteed flow of 35,000 cusecs on the first and last ten days of April and 27,633 cusecs between April 11 and 20. If the Ganga’s flow falls below 50,000 cusecs in any ten-day period, the two governments will enter immediate consultations to make emergency adjustments.

For decades, Bihar’s political leaders have argued that the Ganga water-sharing treaty with Bangladesh does not adequately account for the state’s water needs.

item.title: Are probiotics necessary? Food expert Krish Ashok asks this question in his new book

The global probiotics market is now a multi-billion-dollar industry. A supplement may contain one or several named strains, measured in colony-forming units (CFU) – a laboratory estimate of how many organisms remain capable of growing. Your colon already houses tens of trillions of microbes from hundreds of species, which makes a capsule a rounding error.

A rounding error is not the same as nothing – microbes can influence an ecosystem without becoming its majority. But the marketing claim with the enormous-looking number tells you almost nothing unless that exact strain has been shown to solve a specific problem you have.

A small but striking 2018 Weizmann Institute study tested this directly. Researchers sampled the intestinal wall rather than relying only on stool and found that a standard probiotic mixture behaved very differently between people. In some, the newcomers briefly settled; in others, they passed through like the visitor in Satyajit Ray’s Agantuk.

After antibiotics, that particular probiotic mixture actually delayed the return of the original microbial community compared with leaving it alone, a bit like what happens when politically connected squatters occupy your land. Graham Stuart Staines, a Christian missionary from Australia, dedicated nearly 35 years of his life healing patients of leprosy in the forest interiors of Mayurbhanj district in Odisha. In that impoverished remote forest land, there were none more despised and dispossessed than those living with leprosy. item.title: How the mismatch between climate change and touristic aspirations is harming the Himalayas
item.description: An excerpt from Sonali Gupta’s essay in ‘The Living Himalaya: Rock, Sky, Spirit’, edited by Namita Gokhale and Malashri Lal.
item.content:encoded:
Long before Instagram discovered the “mountain aesthetic”, writers and painters had turned the Himalaya and its connected ranges into screens for every possible longing. James Hilton’s Lost Horizon condensed central and eastern Himalayan motifs into Shangri-La, a timeless sanctuary of moderation and wisdom somewhere beyond the ordinary world.

Nicholas Roerich marched through Kashmir, Ladakh and Central Asia in the 1920s, chasing legends of Shambhala and painting a long series of canvases full of cobalt ridges, luminous snows and monasteries perched like punctuation marks on cliffs. Admirers sometimes say he left hidden clues in these canvases; one suspects the mountains, if asked, would shrug and point out that the most obvious clue is the geology in the background, which everyone compliments and almost no one reads.

Eventually Roerich settled in Naggar in Kullu Valley, building a house that looks modest until you glimpse the views from its verandah. From there he continued to paint the ranges that had once been rumoured as a hidden kingdom, now treated as both subject and neighbour. Between his canvases, his role in early cultural-protection treaties, and the ongoing activity at the Urusvati Himalayan Research Institute, Roerich helped crystallise a vocabulary of Himalayan sacredness that still colours everything...

item.title: Why more people are resorting to ‘DIY’ health advice and it is dangerous

item.content:encoded:
Need treatment fast? Many people now turn to Google before a healthcare professional. From checking symptoms online to buying medicines online and taking advice from social media influencers, healthcare is increasingly becoming a do-it-yourself activity.

Convenience is a big part of the appeal. Information is available instantly – no need to wait weeks to see a GP – and online communities often provide reassurance from people with similar experiences.

Researching a health problem on the internet can feel empowering. But while greater access to health information has benefits, the rise of DIY healthcare also comes with risks. Research suggests that diagnosing and treating yourself, or relying on unqualified sources for advice, can lead to mistakes, the wrong use of medicines and delays in getting professional help.

The internet has changed the way people access health information. A few decades ago, someone worried about a symptom might consult a doctor, pharmacist or medical reference book. Today, a search engine can generate thousands of results in seconds.

item.title: Rage, lust and radical growth: Five must-read menopause novels
item.description: Terms like ‘meno-lit’ and ‘hot flush noir’ are surfacing – just as ‘chick-lit’ was once used to patronise commercial women’s fiction.
item.content:encoded:
Novels featuring older female characters enduring the joint horrors of ageism and misogyny have been around for a while. But fiction foregrounding the specifics of midlife hormonal changes is a surprisingly recent phenomenon.

Given the medical profiles of menopause (and its predecessor, perimenopause), perhaps it’s unsurprising that wellness guides and health-related memoirs have led the way.

Journalist Sam Baker’s pioneering The Shift, actor Naomi Watts’ Dare I Say It and Darcey Steinke’s Flash Count Diary combine personal experience with research. Handbooks like Liz Earle’s The Good Menopause Guide and Dr Mary Claire Havers’ series on perimenopause and menopause focus on disseminating facts.

Now that fiction is catching up, terms like “meno-lit” and “hot flush noir” are surfacing – just as “chick-lit” was once used to patronise commercial women’s fiction. Hopefully, the increasing visibility of menopausal protagonists will move past the novelty phase and become a mainstay of the novel. After all, the stages of menopause are a universal female experience. Surely, it’s time they were integrated into the wider realms of fiction.

item.title: The seven crumbling pillars of India’s democracy
item.description: It is becoming painfully evident that the ailment affecting Indian democracy is not one that a change in government can cure.
item.content:encoded:
A century has passed since the publication of the autobiography of TE Lawrence, popularly known as Lawrence of Arabia. The title Seven Pillars of Wisdom is drawn from the Book of Proverbs in the Bible: “Wisdom hath builded her house, she hath hewn out her seven pillars.”

How appropriate, then, that in their wisdom, the founders of our Constitution went in for democracy as the form of government that would guide independent India’s destiny.

As it transpires, the structure of democracy in India rests on seven pillars, namely (i) legislature (ii) executive (political and bureaucratic) (iii) political parties (iv) judiciary (v) independent institutions (vi) media and (vii) civil society.

As of today, all the pillars appear shaky, threatening the future of democracy, although it could be argued that structural weaknesses in the Indian democratic edifice have existed right from 1947.

item.title: This book revisits the Buddha’s India teachings on living mindfully in the present, past, and future
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Touching the Footsteps of the Buddha’, by Thich Nhat Hanh, edited by Shantum Seth.
item.content:encoded:
To be in the here and in the now is the basic practice of Buddhism. We have talked about how in our daily life, our body may be at one place, but our mind is elsewhere. Our mind may be caught in the regret or sorrow concerning the past, or worries concerning the future. Often, we are locked into the prison of the past and are not able to live the present moment deeply.

item.title: Microsoft offers exit packages to 60,000 employees as it scales up AI investment

item.content:encoded:
Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees in India, Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom as the technology company increases its investments in artificial intelligence, AFP reported.

The latest offer covers about 27% of Microsoft’s global workforce.

Employees at the vice-president level and below were eligible for the offer. Some employees, including those working in data centres, sales and marketing, are excluded from the scheme. Around 30% of those eligible have already opted for the voluntary retirement plan, CNBC reported.

The company has been investing heavily in data centres to meet growing demand for AI computing and provide cloud services to companies including Anthropic and OpenAI.

Amy Coleman, an executive vice-president and chief people officer at Microsoft, said that the voluntary exit offer reflected the company’s efforts to adapt to changing business needs, the news agency reported.

“[We are] creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” AFP quoted Coleman as telling employees in a memo.

Microsoft had 2.23 lakh employees globally at the end of June, down from 2.28 lakh at the end of 2025, AFP reported, citing regulatory filings.

The special intensive revision in West Bengal was carried out ahead of the Assembly elections in April. The final rolls published in February initially excluded more than 61 lakh voters, with the process continuing through supplementary lists and adjudication of about 60 lakh “doubtful and pending” cases.

A book by activist Umar Khalid has been removed from the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Pune library to “avoid any misunderstanding or unrest”, The Indian Express quoted the administration as saying on Sunday.

Khalid has been in prison for more than six years without trial in connection with the 2020 Delhi riots conspiracy case.

The book was removed after a social media account called Gems of Indian Academia shared a photograph showing it as a new addition to the institute’s library, The Indian Express reported.

Madabhushi Madan Gopal, chairperson of the institute’s board of governors, said on social media that he was “shocked” to learn that the book had been added to the library.

“This is retracted last night and action is initiated on those who played this mischief, I assure such things will not happen again in IISER Pune,” he said.

item.title: A documentary revisits Libia Lobo Sardesai’s remarkable contribution to the Goa liberation struggle

item.content:encoded:
Libia Lobo Sardesai is worthy of an international biopic, or a web series at the very least. It isn’t every day that you hear of a young woman who quit a secure job and co-founded an underground radio station to support Goa’s struggle to gain liberation from Portugal. Even rarer is the woman who gathered other achievements like some might pick flowers – a pioneering female lawyer, the founder of the Women’s Cooperative Bank in Goa as well as the Goa College of Home Science.

A recent documentary on Lobo Sardesai, who is now 102, gives some measure of her feats. Libby de Liberdade by Anjali Monteiro and KP Jayasankar is built around the creation of a mural to mark Lobo Sardesai’s birth centenary in 2024. Painted by Solomon Lobo, the grandson of the prominent artist Francis Newton Souza, the mural is situated right across from where Lobo Sardesai lives in Panaji.

The filmmakers also interview Lobo Sardesai at length, and include footage of various celebratory achievements around her. The 79-minute documentary will be screened on October 30 at Mumbai’s Prithvi Theatre by the Vikalp collective.

Peace bonds – legal promises to maintain public peace – are intended to prevent violence. But their use against protesters reiterates that in a democracy, the absence of protest is not proof of public peace.

My mother suffered from bipolar disorder. We didn’t have a name for the illness but we experienced its effects in bizarre ways. One late evening, as I sat doing my homework, my mother came into the room, agitated and manic. She ordered me to get up and follow her to the terrace. She said that I had no redeeming qualities, nothing going for me, nothing to live for. It would be best if I jumped off the roof with her.

Sangeeta Prajapati applied for a Unique Disability Identity number for her 14-year-old daughter, Om Kumari, in April 2025. Since then, she has spent at least five nights at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in South Delhi, seeking appointments with specialist doctors to assess Kumari, who has autism.

The assessments are the most important steps in the generation of the UDID number. In Kumari’s case, doctors need to evaluate her reasoning, learning and problem-solving capabilities, as well as her adaptive behaviour, which covers a range of social skills, and skills required for activities of daily living. item.title: Lula’s ‘miracle’ victory buys time for Brazil, resonates globally amid rise of far-right
item.description: The world’s fourth-largest democracy has now bucked the trend of far-right gains, and is a symbol that democrats elsewhere will not ignore.
item.content:encoded:
Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written.

The far-right presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, had come out of the first round of the presidential election with a lead that looked impossible to overcome.

At 80 years old, Lula seemed headed for a quiet exit after four decades at the centre of Brazilian political life.

On Sunday, however, Lula proved everyone wrong. He won the runoff and secured a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president.

A night of firsts

The election result is unprecedented in Brazilian politics in at least three ways.

First, no Brazilian presidential candidate had ever won the first round and then lost the runoff. Since the two-round system was adopted by the 1988 Brazilian Constitution, the first-round leader had always gone on to win.

Lula broke that pattern by turning a defeat of around 2.2 million votes in the first round into a solid victory, in three weeks.

Second, no Brazilian president has ever been elected to four terms. When his new term ends, Lula will have governed Brazil for 16 (non-consecutive) years – the longest democratically elected tenure in the country’s history.

item.content:encoded:
Kalaripayattu

is an art.
is warfare.
is a way of living.
is in my blood.
is all I have ever known.
is Kannappa Chekavar.

Kannappa Chekavar

is my acha,
my father.

He is disciplined and strict.
He is loving and encouraging too.

He is also the greatest
Kalari master of Kadathanadu.

He is unmatchable,
unbeatable
in this art of war
fought with every weapon used in close combat.
Wooden staffs, swords, daggers, maces
are mere toys in his hands.

It is said he knows more adavukkal – combat moves –
than anyone else practising Kalaripayattu.
It is also said
that he has never taught
all nineteen of them to anyone.

He has shared all
but the last technique,
the most cunning one,
keeping it close to his heart,
waiting for that special student
worthy enough to earn this secret.

No pity

The consequence of being ten minutes late
is an extra hour of practice.

Breathless and exhausted,
I gaze longingly
at the other students leaving the class.
They must be off to the vacant field
by the village pond
to hang out and play
before the sun sets for the day.

Aromal steps out too,

Control your breathing, Unniarcha!

item.title: Centre amends rules to allow E100 fuel in compatible vehicles
item.description: The modified rules allow flex-fuel vehicles to run on nearly 100% ethanol, alongside E85, which contains 85% ethanol and 15% petrol.
item.content:encoded:
The Union government has amended rules to allow vehicles designed for flex-fuel to run on E100, a fuel made up of nearly 100% ethanol.

The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways issued the notification amending the Motor Vehicles Rules on Friday. The changes came into effect on Monday.

The modified rules allow flex-fuel vehicles to run on E100 alongside E85, which contains 85% ethanol and 15% petrol.

Flex-fuel vehicles can run on different blends of petrol and ethanol. However, regular petrol vehicles, including those designed to run on E20 fuel, which contains 20% ethanol and 80% petrol, cannot use E85 or E100, Hindustan Times reported.

Under its Ethanol Blended Petrol programme, the government mandates that all petrol sold in the country be blended with 20% ethanol – a substance produced from sugarcane and food grain. The policy is aimed at reducing India’s dependency on fossil fuels, cutting greenhouse gas emissions and boosting income for sugarcane farmers.

However, consumers have complained that the new fuel mix damages engines and reduces their mileage.

An opinion poll by LocalCircles published on July 5 showed that 53% of the surveyed petrol vehicle owners said that they believe that the government’s handling of the E20 rollout was “disastrous” or “ineffective”.
